# [Coding/Content] Hd

## Aliases

- Hd
- human detail
- partial human

## Definition

`Hd` is coded when the response describes only a part of a human figure.  
There is not a whole person, but a bodily detail or human fragment.

## Conditions

- The main content has to be a part of a person rather than a whole figure.
- The part must be understood as realistically human.
- Typical examples are an arm, hand, leg, fingers, head, or incomplete torso.
- If the response builds a whole person, go back to [scoring-input/contents/H](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FH).

## Cautions

- `Hd` is not the same as [scoring-input/contents/H](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FH); there is no whole human figure here.
- `Hd` is not the same as [scoring-input/contents/(Hd)](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2F%28Hd%29); `(Hd)` is reserved for a fantastic or mythic human detail.
- `Hd` often pushes human representation toward poorer quality, so it is worth reviewing [scoring-input/gphr/PHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FPHR).
- `Hd` is also not the same as [scoring-input/contents/Hx](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHx); `Hx` codes human experience, not a body fragment.

`Hh` is coded when the main content is a household utensil or domestic object.  
The key point is that the form is understood as something used in the home, not as clothing and not as artwork by itself.

- `Hh` does not cover clothing; for that, reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Cg](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FCg).
- `Hh` and [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt) may come close, but they are not equivalent.
- `Hh` and [scoring-input/contents/Ad](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAd) only overlap when the same household object is described as being made from an animal part.

If the object is mainly understood as decorative or artistic, it may also require scoring-input/contents/Art.

If the person stresses that the object is made from an animal part, it may coexist with scoring-input/contents/Ad.
[Cautions] Hh does not cover clothing; for that, reconsider scoring-input/contents/Cg.

Hh and scoring-input/contents/Art may come close, but they are not equivalent.

Hh and scoring-input/contents/Ad only overlap when the same household object is described as being made from an animal part.

# [Coding/Content] Hx

## Aliases

- Hx
- human experience
- human feeling

## Definition

`Hx` is coded when the response assigns a clearly human feeling, sensation, or experience rather than a human figure as such.  
The focus is on human experience that is explicitly attributed.

## Conditions

- The person must clearly attribute an emotion, internal state, or sensory human experience.
- That attribution has to be unmistakable, not merely hinted at.
- `Hx` may appear as a secondary content code when a figure clearly expresses a human experience.
- In poorly formed `M` responses that directly symbolize human experience, it is also worth reviewing [scoring-input/special-score/AB](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAB).

## Cautions

- `Hx` is not the same as [scoring-input/contents/H](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FH) or [scoring-input/contents/Hd](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHd); those codes describe figures, not experiences.
- Vague phrases like "looks angry" or "kind of tired" are not always enough; the attribution has to be genuinely clear.
- `Hx` may be primary or secondary depending on the response, but it should not be assigned from examiner impression alone.
- When the response symbolically represents human experience, review [scoring-input/special-score/AB](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAB) as well.

# [Coding/Content] Id

## Aliases

- Id
- idiographic content
- idiosyncratic content

## Definition

`Id` is used as a last-resort content code when the response does not reasonably fit standard content categories.  
It is not a code for "odd content" in general; it is for truly idiographic content after other options have been checked.

## Conditions

- Consider `Id` only after checking that the response does not fit another content category better.
- When it is used, it is good practice to preserve the exact wording of the content in writing.
- If the unusual content is really scientific or technical, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Sc](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FSc).
- If the unusual content takes the form of an artistic or symbolic object, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt).

## Cautions

- Strange content does not automatically become `Id`.
- A test tube, machine, or device should still go first to [scoring-input/contents/Sc](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FSc).
- A decorative or symbolic object may require [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt) instead of `Id`.
- `Id` should remain a controlled exception, not a convenient category for uncertainty.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Content] Contents](ref://scoring-input/contents)
- [[Coding/Content] Sc](ref://scoring-input/contents/Sc)
- [[Coding/Content] Art](ref://scoring-input/contents/Art)

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Content] Ls

## Aliases

- Ls
- landscape
- scenery

## Definition

`Ls` is coded when the main content is a landscape, geographic view, or broad natural scene.  
The focus has to be on the scene or setting, not just on a single plant or object.

## Conditions

- Use it for mountains, coast, valley, horizon, riverbank, rocky landscape, or another response understood as a natural view.
- It requires that the person see a scene or spatial expanse, not just an isolated botanical detail.
- If the response describes a map or cartographic representation, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Ge](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FGe).
- If the response points to general nature or natural environment rather than a bounded landscape, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Na](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FNa).
- If `Na` applies with `Ls`, record `Na` only and do not add `Ls`.
- If `Na` is absent but both `Bt` and `Ls` apply, record only the one that best represents the response.

## Cautions

- `Ls` is not the same as [scoring-input/contents/Ge](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FGe), which is reserved for maps or cartographic reference.
- `Na` takes priority whenever it applies with `Ls`.
- If the focus falls on a specific plant, branch, or botanical form, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Bt](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FBt).

## Cross References

# [Coding/Content] Na

## Aliases

- Na
- nature
- natural environment

## Definition

`Na` is coded for a natural environment, natural phenomenon, or general nature setting that is not better coded as botany or a specific landscape.  
The response points to "nature" as a whole rather than to one isolated object.

## Conditions

- Use it for the sun, moon, a planet, sky, water, ocean, lake, river, ice, snow, rain, fog, mist, rainbow, storm, tornado, night, or a raindrop.
- The focus has to stay on the natural setting or phenomenon itself.
- If `Na` appears together with [scoring-input/contents/Bt](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FBt) or [scoring-input/contents/Ls](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FLs), code `Na` only; do not also code `Bt` or `Ls`.
- If `Na` is absent but both `Bt` and `Ls` apply, choose only the one that best represents the response.
- If the person describes a cloud, first reconsider [scoring-input/contents/Cl](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FCl); fog and mist are coded `Na`.

## Cautions

- `Na` takes priority over [scoring-input/contents/Bt](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FBt) and [scoring-input/contents/Ls](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FLs); these three codes are not combined in one response.
- `Na` is not used for a map; that belongs to [scoring-input/contents/Ge](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FGe).
- An isolated botanical detail does not justify `Na` by itself if the response is not describing general nature.

# [Coding/Content] Sc

## Aliases

- Sc
- science
- scientific object
- technical object

## Definition

`Sc` is coded when the content is understood as scientific, technical, mechanical, or technological.  
The important point is that the person sees an apparatus, instrument, machine, or product of applied science.

## Conditions

- Use it for microscope, robot, machine, weapon, vehicle, technical device, laboratory instrument, or other scientific apparatus.
- It can also include ordinary technology when the response treats it as a device or mechanism.
- If the object has an artistic or decorative presentation, `Sc` may coexist with [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt).
- Before sending an unusual response to [scoring-input/contents/Id](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FId), first test whether it fits `Sc`.

## Cautions

- `Sc` does not mean merely "strange"; it requires a scientific or technical reading.
- An unusual object such as a test tube, engine, or machine part still belongs under `Sc`, not automatically under [scoring-input/contents/Id](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FId).
- If the response emphasizes cultural symbol or aesthetic piece, it may require [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt) in addition to `Sc`.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Content] Contents](ref://scoring-input/contents)

# [Coding/Content] Sx

## Aliases

- Sx
- sex
- sexual content

## Definition

`Sx` is coded when the content includes a sexual organ, sexual activity, or explicit sexual meaning.  
It often works as a secondary content code alongside a human or anatomy code.

## Conditions

- Use it for genitals, sexualized breasts, intercourse, sexual act, or another direct sexual reference.
- The sexual content has to be actually present in the response and not inferred only by the examiner.
- It is often added together with [scoring-input/contents/H](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FH), [scoring-input/contents/Hd](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHd), or [scoring-input/contents/An](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAn).
- If the response only indicates nudity or body form without clear sexual meaning, do not code `Sx` automatically.

## Cautions

- `Sx` has to be separated from [scoring-input/contents/An](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAn), which centers on anatomy rather than sexuality.
- `Sx` does not by itself equal whole human content; it may need [scoring-input/contents/H](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FH) or [scoring-input/contents/Hd](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHd).
- Coding requires explicit sexual content, not an examiner's unsupported insinuation.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Content] Contents](ref://scoring-input/contents)

- [[Coding/Content] Hd](ref://scoring-input/contents/Hd)

# [Coding/Content] Xy

## Aliases

- Xy
- x-ray
- radiograph

## Definition

`Xy` is coded when the content is perceived as an X-ray or radiographic image.  
If the response is coded `Xy`, the focus is on the radiographic way of seeing the object.

- Use it for an X-ray, radiographic plate, internal image seen explicitly as an X-ray, or another radiographic study.

## Cautions

- `Xy` is not the same as [scoring-input/contents/An](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAn); `An` points to anatomy and `Xy` points to radiographic format.
- If the person only names bone, organ, or internal body structure without saying it is an X-ray, first reconsider `An`.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] Determinants
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] Determinants

## Aliases

- Determinants
- determinant coding
- movement
- chromatic color
- duplicate movement-family input

## Definition

Determinants code what aspect of the blot makes the response look the way it does.
They do not code what the person sees, but why it appears that way: form, movement, color, shading, reflection, or dimension.

## Conditions

- The coding decision must be based on the person's words and inquiry, not on free examiner inference.
- A response may contain more than one determinant if the person actually uses more than one blot feature.
- Multiple determinants may coexist, but active and passive codes from the same movement family are not entered in separate slots. Record only one of `a`, `p`, or `a-p` for each human, animal, or inanimate movement family.
- Do not record more than one form-emphasis category for the same determinant in one response. Within `FC/CF/C`, `FC'/C'F/C'`, `FT/TF/T`, `FV/VF/V`, `FY/YF/Y`, or `Fr/rF`, record only one code; if more than one seems applicable, use the category with the least form emphasis. Different shading kinds may coexist when they are based on distinct wording or blot features.
- When a complex response combines determinants, code them in the order they appear in the response phase.
- The main determinant families are movement [scoring-input/determinants/M](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FM), [scoring-input/determinants/FM](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFM), [scoring-input/determinants/m](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2Fm); chromatic color [scoring-input/determinants/FC](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC), [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF), [scoring-input/determinants/C](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC), [scoring-input/determinants/Cn](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCn); achromatic color [scoring-input/determinants/FC'](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC'), [scoring-input/determinants/C'F](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC'F), [scoring-input/determinants/C'](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC'); texture [scoring-input/determinants/FT](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFT), [scoring-input/determinants/TF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FTF), [scoring-input/determinants/T](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FT); vista [scoring-input/determinants/FV](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFV), [scoring-input/determinants/VF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FVF), [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV); diffuse shading [scoring-input/determinants/FY](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFY), [scoring-input/determinants/YF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FYF), [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY); pure form [scoring-input/determinants/F](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FF); reflection [scoring-input/determinants/Fr](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFr), [scoring-input/determinants/rF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FrF); and form-based dimension [scoring-input/determinants/FD](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFD).

## Cautions

- Determinants do not replace [scoring-input/fq](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq) or location; those are separate coding axes.
- In chromatic color, the key question is whether form or color carries the main weight. That distinction separates `FC`, `CF`, and `C`.
- In achromatic color, the same logic reappears with `FC'`, `C'F`, and `C'`, but the relevant cue is black, white, or gray functioning as color.
- `Cn` is not full color responding. It marks color naming without true determinant-level color use.
- In movement, the key question is what kind of action is attributed: human, animal, or inanimate.
- In texture, vista, and diffuse shading, the key question is whether form leads, the sensory quality leads, or form is too weak for a mixed code.
- Texture, vista, and diffuse shading should not be collapsed into one broad shading family. They separate tactile surface, depth/relief, and vague shaded experience.
- In pure form and reflection coding, the key question is whether the response depends only on shape, on mirror/reflection quality, or on depth created by formal arrangement.
- The same word should not be coded twice to justify multiple determinants of the same type.
- Black, white, or gray wording alone is not enough for achromatic color coding; it has to function as color rather than as shading, vista, or diffuse darkness.

[Title] [Coding/Determinants] Determinants
[Aliases] Determinants, determinant coding, movement, chromatic color, achromatic color, texture, vista, diffuse shading
[Definition] Determinants code what aspect of the blot makes the response look the way it does.
They do not code what the person sees, but why it appears that way: form, movement, color, shading, reflection, or dimension.
[Conditions] The coding decision must be based on the person's words and inquiry, not on free examiner inference.

A response may contain more than one determinant if the person actually uses more than one blot feature.

Multiple determinants may coexist, but active and passive codes from the same movement family are not entered in separate slots. Record only one of a, p, or a-p for each human, animal, or inanimate movement family.

Do not record more than one form-emphasis category for the same determinant in one response. Within FC/CF/C, FC'/C'F/C', FT/TF/T, FV/VF/V, FY/YF/Y, or Fr/rF, record only one code; if more than one seems applicable, use the category with the least form emphasis. Different shading kinds may coexist when they are based on distinct wording or blot features.

When a complex response combines determinants, code them in the order they appear in the response phase.

The main determinant families are movement scoring-input/determinants/M, scoring-input/determinants/FM, scoring-input/determinants/m; chromatic color scoring-input/determinants/FC, scoring-input/determinants/CF, scoring-input/determinants/C, scoring-input/determinants/Cn; achromatic color scoring-input/determinants/FC', scoring-input/determinants/C'F, scoring-input/determinants/C'; texture scoring-input/determinants/FT, scoring-input/determinants/TF, scoring-input/determinants/T; vista scoring-input/determinants/FV, scoring-input/determinants/VF, scoring-input/determinants/V; diffuse shading scoring-input/determinants/FY, scoring-input/determinants/YF, scoring-input/determinants/Y; pure form scoring-input/determinants/F; reflection scoring-input/determinants/Fr, scoring-input/determinants/rF; and form-based dimension scoring-input/determinants/FD.
[Cautions] Determinants do not replace scoring-input/fq or location; those are separate coding axes.

In chromatic color, the key question is whether form or color carries the main weight. That distinction separates FC, CF, and C.

In achromatic color, the same logic reappears with FC', C'F, and C', but the relevant cue is black, white, or gray functioning as color.

Cn is not full color responding. It marks color naming without true determinant-level color use.

In movement, the key question is what kind of action is attributed: human, animal, or inanimate.

In texture, vista, and diffuse shading, the key question is whether form leads, the sensory quality leads, or form is too weak for a mixed code.

Texture, vista, and diffuse shading should not be collapsed into one broad shading family. They separate tactile surface, depth/relief, and vague shaded experience.

In pure form and reflection coding, the key question is whether the response depends only on shape, on mirror/reflection quality, or on depth created by formal arrangement.

The same word should not be coded twice to justify multiple determinants of the same type.

Black, white, or gray wording alone is not enough for achromatic color coding; it has to function as color rather than as shading, vista, or diffuse darkness.

Interpretive use of these codes is reviewed later in variables such as result-interpretation/lower-section/affect/FC\_CF\_C, result-interpretation/lower-section/affect/PureC, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/Lambda, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumCprime, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumT, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumV, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumY, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/FM, result-interpretation/lower-section/core/m, result-interpretation/lower-section/selfPerception/Fr\_rF, or result-interpretation/lower-section/selfPerception/FD.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] C
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] C

## Aliases

- C
- pure color
- color without form

## Definition

`C` is used when chromatic color alone determines the response and form does not genuinely participate.
It is pure color responding.

## Conditions

- Chromatic color is the basis of the response.
- Form does not make a real coding contribution.
- The response is more purely color-driven than [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF).

## Cautions

- `C` should not be used if form still contributes secondarily; in that case, use [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF).
- `C` is not assigned just because a colorful answer sounds emotional; the response has to depend on color itself.
- Interpretively, `C` belongs to the chromatic color family and should later be read together with `FC` and `CF`.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] C'
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] C'

## Aliases

- C'
- pure achromatic color
- achromatic color without form

## Definition

`C'` is used when the response depends exclusively on achromatic color in the blot.
There is not enough formal support, and black, white, or gray clearly function as color.

## Conditions

- The response is based on black, white, or gray used as color.
- There is not enough formal organization for `FC'` or `C'F`.
- If inquiry shows real secondary form, reconsider `C'F`.
- The decision requires clear and unmistakable achromatic color use.
- Because `C'` is a pure achromatic determinant without form, record its Form Quality as `FQnone`.

## Cautions

- `C'` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/C](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC); both are pure color, but one is achromatic and the other chromatic.
- Many achromatic cue words also occur in shading. Confirm that they function as color.
- If the response points to depth or distance, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If the response points to diffuse shading, darkness, or atmospheric tone, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] C'F

## Aliases

- C'F
- achromatic color-form
- achromatic color with secondary form

## Definition

`C'F` is used when achromatic color dominates the response and form remains secondary.
The response depends more on black, white, or gray used as color than on formal organization.

## Conditions

- The person uses achromatic features as the primary basis of the response.
- Some formal support is present, but clearly secondary.
- If form carries the main weight, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/FC'](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC').
- If no real form support is present, [scoring-input/determinants/C'](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC') may fit better.

## Cautions

- `C'F` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF); both the type of color and the perceptual basis differ.
- Saying black, white, or gray does not by itself require `C'F`.
- If the response depends more on distance or relief, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If the response is mainly indefinite, murky, or diffuse shading, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] CF
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] CF

## Aliases

- CF
- color-form
- form secondary to color

## Definition

`CF` is used when chromatic color is more important than form, but form still contributes secondarily.
The response is color-driven, yet not completely free of form.

## Conditions

- Chromatic color carries the main weight of the response.
- Form still contributes enough to keep the response from being pure color.
- If form clearly dominates, use [scoring-input/determinants/FC](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC).
- If form does not genuinely participate, use [scoring-input/determinants/C](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC).

## Cautions

- `CF` is not assigned just because the person mentions color. Color has to lead the percept.
- The distinction from `FC` depends on which aspect the person relies on more heavily.
- `CF` still differs from `C` because form remains present at a secondary level.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] Cn
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] Cn

## Aliases

- Cn
- color naming
- named color

## Definition

`Cn` is used when the person names a color, but does not use color as a true determinant of the response.
That is why `Cn` does not belong to the full chromatic family `C / CF / FC` as a full color code.

## Conditions

- The person explicitly mentions a color.
- That mention does not support the main perceptual construction of the response.
- The object would remain the same even if the color reference were removed.
- If color truly participates in the response, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/FC](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC), [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF), or [scoring-input/determinants/C](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC).

## Cautions

- `Cn` is not the same as `C`. In `C`, color is a true determinant; in `Cn`, color is only named.
- A casual color mention should not be inflated into `FC` or `CF` if the response does not depend on it.
- `Cn` should not be counted interpretively as if it were full chromatic color.
- When in doubt, ask whether color makes it look like that, or whether the person is only describing an accessory feature.

**Downstream calculation boundary:** The conventional lower-section label remains `FC:CF+C`, but this displayed ratio uses `FC:(CF+C+Cn)`. A coded `Cn` therefore increases the displayed right side by one. This display convention must not be reused as a general chromatic-color total: `WSumC`, S-CON criterion `CF+C > FC`, and Color-Shading blend counts exclude `Cn` and retain their own formulas.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] F
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] F

## Aliases

- F
- pure form
- form only

## Definition

`F` is coded when the response is supported only by form.  
There is no operative use of movement, color, reflection, texture, vista, or additional dimension.

## Conditions

- Form must be the only explicit basis of the response.
- During inquiry, the person must still rely on contour, outline, or formal configuration.
- If another genuine determinant appears, `F` by itself is no longer enough.
- Final coding must follow what the person said, not free examiner inference.

## Cautions

- `F` is not the same as [scoring-input/fq](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq); `F` is a determinant and `FQ` is form quality.
- If the response includes depth created by contour or relative size, review [scoring-input/determinants/FD](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFD).
- If the response adds texture, vista, or diffuse shading, review [scoring-input/determinants/FT](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFT), [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV), or [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).
- A response can include `F` inside a more complex combination, but that does not remove the need to decide whether another determinant actually dominates.

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] FC

## Aliases

- FC
- form-color
- color secondary to form

## Definition

`FC` is used when the response is based mainly on form and chromatic color remains secondary.
Color is present, but the person organizes the response chiefly through formal features.

## Conditions

- Form guides the main identification of the object.
- Chromatic color participates in the response, but with secondary importance.
- If color appears more dominant than form, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/CF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FCF).
- If form is not really used, [scoring-input/determinants/C](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC) may fit better.

## Cautions

- `FC` does not mean merely that color is present in the card; color has to take part in a form-dominated response.
- The key distinction from `CF` is which aspect carries the main weight.
- Some responses first appear to be `CF`, but later clarification shows that form dominates and `FC` is correct.
- The interpretive use of this family is reviewed later in [result-interpretation/lower-section/affect/FC_CF_C](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Faffect%2FFC_CF_C).

# [Coding/Determinants] FC'

## Aliases

- FC'
- achromatic form-color
- form with achromatic color

## Definition

`FC'` is used when form organizes the response and achromatic color remains secondary.
Black, white, or gray features must function clearly as color, not merely as shading or area description.

## Conditions

- Form supports the main identification of the object.
- Achromatic features participate as color, but with secondary weight.
- If achromatic color dominates the response, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/C'F](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC'F).
- If there is little or no real form support, [scoring-input/determinants/C'](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FC') may fit better.

## Cautions

- `FC'` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/FC](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC); the first uses achromatic color, the second chromatic color.
- Words like black, white, gray, light, or dark are not enough by themselves; they must function as color.
- If the response points more to depth or distance, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If the response points more to vague atmosphere, darkness, or diffuse distress, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] FD
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] FD

## Aliases

- FD
- form-dimension
- form-based depth

## Definition

`FD` is coded when the impression of depth, distance, or dimension comes from form and contour rather than shading.  
The person organizes the third dimension from relative size, position, or formal arrangement.

## Conditions

- The dimensional quality must come from formal relations of size, edge, distance, or contour.
- The response should not depend on shading to produce depth.
- Inquiry must confirm that the idea of relief, distance, or perspective comes from form.
- If the dimension depends on shading, review [scoring-input/determinants/FV](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFV), [scoring-input/determinants/VF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FVF), or [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).

## Cautions

- `FD` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/F](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FF); `FD` adds dimensional organization.
- `FD` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/FV](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFV) or [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV); those responses do depend on shading.
- `FD` is also not the same as content [scoring-input/contents/Fd](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FFd); one is a determinant and the other is content.
- Phrases like "farther away," "closer," "coming out," or "behind" are not enough by themselves if they are not supported by form or contour.

## Cross References

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] FM

## Aliases

- FM
- animal movement
- nonhuman movement

## Definition

`FM` is used when the response implies ordinary animal movement.
It covers movement that fits the expected action pattern of the animal or nonhuman creature.

## Input Code Rule

`FM` is the family label used in Structural Summary totals. For an individual response, enter `FMa`, `FMp`, or `FMa-p` according to its active/passive quality. Bare `FM` is not a complete response code.
Use only one animal-movement code in a response. If separate animal objects show active and passive movement, enter `FMa-p` once rather than entering `FMa` and `FMp` in separate slots. One object showing both is not automatically `FMa-p`; review which movement governs the coding.

## Conditions

- The perceived action is movement.
- The action belongs to an animal or nonhuman creature acting in a species-appropriate way.
- The response does not show clearly human or anthropomorphic movement.

## Cautions

- If the action is genuinely human or anthropomorphic, use [scoring-input/determinants/M](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FM).
- If the movement belongs to an inanimate object, use [scoring-input/determinants/m](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2Fm).
- Animal content alone is not enough. There has to be perceived movement.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Determinants] M](ref://scoring-input/determinants/M)
- [[Coding/Determinants] m](ref://scoring-input/determinants/m)

# [Coding/Determinants] FT

## Aliases

- FT
- form-texture
- texture secondary

## Definition

`FT` is coded when form organizes the response and texture stays secondary.  
The tactile or surface quality is present, but the response still rests first on form.

## Conditions

- Form identifies the main object.
- The person then adds a tactile, surface, or texture quality.
- The texture cue has to be genuinely stated in the response or inquiry.
- If texture carries more weight than form, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/TF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FTF).

## Cautions

- `FT` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/TF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FTF); the difference is which feature dominates.
- If there is not a real tactile component, the response may remain [scoring-input/determinants/F](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FF).
- If the dominant experience is depth or relief, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If the dominant experience is vague shaded atmosphere, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

# [Coding/Determinants] Fr

## Aliases

- Fr
- form-reflection
- reflection secondary

## Definition

`Fr` is coded when form organizes the response first and the person also describes the object as a reflection or mirror image.  
Symmetry has to be involved, and the idea of reflection must be explicitly present.

## Conditions

- Form has to identify the main object first.
- The person must talk about reflection, mirroring, or an equivalent idea.
- The two objects must be explicitly or implicitly identical.
- If there are only two similar objects because of symmetry, without reflection language, reconsider [scoring-input/pair](ref://scoring-input%2Fpair).

## Cautions

- `Fr` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/rF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FrF); in `Fr`, form stays more clearly dominant.
- `Fr` does not replace the pair code; when there is reflection, do not also add [scoring-input/pair](ref://scoring-input%2Fpair).
- If the response only says there are two matching figures, but does not describe reflection or mirroring, `Fr` does not fit.

en.title: [Coding/Determinants] M
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] M

## Aliases

- M
- human movement
- anthropomorphic movement

## Definition

`M` is used when the response implies human or anthropomorphic activity.
It also applies to animals or fictional figures if they are acting in a genuinely human way.

## Input Code Rule

`M` is the family label used in Structural Summary totals. For an individual response, enter `Ma`, `Mp`, or `Ma-p` according to its active/passive quality. Bare `M` is not a complete response code.
Use only one human-movement code in a response. If separate human objects show active and passive movement, enter `Ma-p` once rather than entering `Ma` and `Mp` in separate slots. One object showing both is not automatically `Ma-p`; review which movement governs the coding.

## Conditions

- The perceived action must be human or clearly anthropomorphic.
- Active and passive actions both qualify, such as fighting, thinking, sleeping, looking, or leaning.
- If an animal performs an action improper to its species and the activity is human, code `M`.
- Base the decision on what the person describes, not on added examiner interpretation.

## Cautions

- Ordinary animal movement is [scoring-input/determinants/FM](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFM), not `M`.
- Movement of inanimate objects is [scoring-input/determinants/m](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2Fm), not `M`.
- Human content alone is not enough. There has to be perceived activity.
- If the response also includes cooperative or aggressive interaction, it may also receive [scoring-input/special-score/COP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCOP) or [scoring-input/special-score/AG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAG).

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] T

## Aliases

- T
- pure texture
- texture only

## Definition

`T` is coded when the response depends on texture without enough form support.  
The tactile or surface quality is the central determinant and form does not truly organize the percept.

## Conditions

- The response grows out of a tactile or surface quality.
- There is not enough form support for `FT` or `TF`.
- Texture must be clearly stated by the person.
- If inquiry shows secondary form organization, reconsider `TF`.

## Cautions

- `T` is not just any sensory wording; real determinant-level texture use is required.
- If depth or relief is primary, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If the dominant experience is vague or diffuse shading, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).
- If form organizes the object, pure `T` no longer fits.

# [Coding/Determinants] TF

## Aliases

- TF
- texture-form
- texture dominant

## Definition

`TF` is coded when texture dominates the response and form stays secondary.  
The tactile or surface experience carries more weight than the formal structure of the percept.

## Conditions

- The response starts from a tactile or surface impression.
- Form participates, but only secondarily.
- If form carries the main load, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/FT](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFT).
- If formal organization is barely present, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/T](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FT).

## Cautions

- `TF` should not be assigned because of one isolated tactile word; the overall emphasis matters.
- If texture is not truly used, the response should not be inflated to `TF`.
- If depth or relief dominates, review [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).
- If diffuse shading dominates, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

# [Coding/Determinants] V

## Aliases

- V
- pure vista
- vista only

## Definition

`V` is coded when the response depends on depth or relief without enough form support.  
The dimensional experience dominates on its own and form does not truly organize the percept.

## Conditions

- The response grows out of distance, depth, or relief.
- There is not enough form support for `FV` or `VF`.
- Inquiry must show that the dimensional quality is really part of the person's response.
- If secondary form support appears, reconsider `VF`.

## Cautions

- `V` is not the same as Card `V`; the symbol is shared, but the context is different.
- If the response depends more on texture, review [scoring-input/determinants/T](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FT).
- If the response depends more on diffuse shading or vague darkness, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).
- The interpretive use of this family returns later in [result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumV](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fcore%2FSumV).

# [Coding/Determinants] VF

## Aliases

- VF
- vista-form
- vista dominant

## Definition

`VF` is coded when depth or dimensionality dominates the response and form stays secondary.  
There is still some form support, but the dimensional quality carries more weight than the formal structure.

## Conditions

- The main impression is depth, distance, or relief.
- Form participates only secondarily.
- If form ends up organizing the response, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/FV](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFV).
- If formal support is barely present, reconsider [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV).

## Cautions

- `VF` should not be confused with [scoring-input/determinants/TF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FTF); one points to dimension and the other to texture.
- If tactile surface quality is more central, review `TF`.
- If the response depends more on diffuse shaded vagueness, review [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY).

# [Coding/Determinants] Y

## Aliases

- Y
- pure shading
- diffuse shading only

## Definition

`Y` is coded when the response depends on diffuse shading without enough form support.  
The dominant experience is vague, shaded, or cloudy, and form does not truly organize the percept.

## Conditions

- The response grows out of shading, darkness, or diffuse uncertainty.
- There is not enough form support for `FY` or `YF`.
- Inquiry must confirm that shading is the real basis of the response.
- If some secondary form support appears, reconsider `YF`.

## Cautions

- `Y` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/V](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FV); one points to diffuse shading and the other to depth.
- `Y` is also not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/T](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FT); one points to shading and the other to texture.
- If the response uses real secondary form support, pure `Y` no longer fits.
- The interpretive use of this family returns later in [result-interpretation/lower-section/core/SumY](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fcore%2FSumY).

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] m

## Aliases

- m
- inanimate movement
- passive movement of object

## Definition

`m` is used when the response implies movement of an inanimate object or passive movement not coded as human or animal movement.
It reflects mechanical, driven, or object-based movement.

## Input Code Rule

`m` is the family label used in Structural Summary totals. For an individual response, enter `ma`, `mp`, or `ma-p` according to its active/passive quality. Bare `m` is not a complete response code.
Use only one inanimate-movement code in a response. If separate inanimate objects show active and passive movement, enter `ma-p` once rather than entering `ma` and `mp` in separate slots. One object showing both is not automatically `ma-p`; review which movement governs the coding.

## Conditions

- The perceived action is movement.
- The mover is inanimate, mechanical, or object-based.
- The movement does not qualify as human or ordinary animal movement.

## Cautions

- If the movement is human or anthropomorphic, use [scoring-input/determinants/M](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FM).

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Determinants] rF

## Aliases

- rF
- reflection-form
- reflection dominant

## Definition

`rF` is coded when the impression of reflection or mirror image dominates the response and form stays secondary.  
Symmetry is still required, but the main emphasis falls on reflectiveness itself.

## Conditions

- The person must explicitly describe a reflection, mirror, or reflected image.
- The reflective impression must organize the response first.
- Form is still present, but with secondary weight.
- If there are only two matching objects because of symmetry, without reflection language, reconsider [scoring-input/pair](ref://scoring-input%2Fpair).

## Cautions

- `rF` is not the same as [scoring-input/determinants/Fr](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFr); in `rF`, the reflection idea carries more weight.
- `rF` is also not the same as [scoring-input/pair](ref://scoring-input%2Fpair); pair requires symmetric identity, but not necessarily a reflected image.
- If the concrete form of the object is clearer than the reflective quality, `Fr` may fit better.
- Reflection is coded within determinants and is not combined with the pair code.

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Developmental Quality] DQ

## Aliases

- DQ
- Developmental Quality
- developmental quality coding

## Definition

Developmental Quality (`DQ`) codes how organized or elaborated the response is as a percept.
It focuses on the structural level of the response, not on whether the form fit is good or poor.

## Conditions

- Choose one DQ code for each scorable response.
- Decide whether the response shows meaningful synthesis.
- Decide whether at least one involved object requires specific form demand.
- Use the four-code set: `+`, `v/+`, `o`, `v`.

## Cautions

- `DQ` is not the same as [scoring-input/fq](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq). `DQ` is about organization; `FQ` is about form quality.
- The same symbol can mean something different in another family. For example, [scoring-input/dq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2F%2B) is not the same construct as [scoring-input/fq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F%2B).
- DQ should be assigned from the response structure itself, not from later interpretation.

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Developmental Quality] +

## Aliases

- DQ+
- synthesized response (+)
- synthesis with formal demand

## Definition

`DQ+` is assigned when the response synthesizes two or more separate but meaningfully related objects, and at least one of those objects requires specific form demand.
The key is not just “more than one object,” but an organized whole.

## Conditions

- More than one distinct object or part is present in the response.
- The objects are meaningfully related to each other.
- At least one involved object requires specific form demand.
- The synthesis feels organized rather than merely listed side by side.

## Cautions

- Two objects that only mirror each other, without meaningful integration, usually do not justify `DQ+`; that pattern more often fits [scoring-input/dq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fo).
- If synthesis is present but none of the objects requires specific form demand, use [scoring-input/dq/v/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fv%2F%2B).
- `DQ+` is not the same as [scoring-input/fq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F%2B). `DQ+` is about organization; `FQ+` is about form quality.

# [Coding/Developmental Quality] o

## Aliases

- DQo
- ordinary developmental quality
- single object with formal demand

## Definition

`DQo` is used when the response does not reach meaningful synthesis, but the object still requires specific form demand.
It reflects an ordinary, non-synthesized level of structural development.

## Conditions

- The response is not an organized synthesis of multiple meaningful objects.
- The percept still depends on specific form demand.
- The object is structured enough to be more than vague impression.
- The response stays at a single-object or non-synthesized level.

## Cautions

- If meaningful synthesis is present and at least one object requires specific form demand, use [scoring-input/dq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2F%2B).
- If synthesis is present without specific form demand, use [scoring-input/dq/v/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fv%2F%2B).
- If the response stays vague and non-synthesized, use [scoring-input/dq/v](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fv).

# [Coding/Developmental Quality] v

## Aliases

- DQv
- vague developmental quality
- vague non-synthesized response

## Definition

`DQv` is used when the response remains vague and does not show meaningful synthesis.
It is the least structurally developed DQ code in the standard four-code set.

## Conditions

- No meaningful synthesis is present.
- The percept does not require specific form demand.
- The response remains comparatively diffuse or impressionistic.
- The response does not fit `DQo`, `DQv/+`, or `DQ+`.

## Cautions

- If the object requires specific form demand but synthesis is absent, use [scoring-input/dq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fo).
- If synthesis is present without specific form demand, use [scoring-input/dq/v/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fv%2F%2B).
- If synthesis is present with specific form demand, use [scoring-input/dq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2F%2B).

en.title: [Coding/Form Quality] FQ
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Form Quality] FQ

## Aliases

- Form Quality
- FQ
- `+`, `o`, `u`, `-`, `none`

## Definition

Form Quality (`FQ`) codes how well the described object fits the contours of the blot.
It is about formal fit, not about the organizational level of the response.

## Conditions

- Place the FQ symbol at the end of the determinant block.
- Use the five-code set: `+`, `o`, `u`, `-`, `none`.
- Base the decision on the form quality table first, then on extrapolation and fit judgment when needed.
- Ask whether the object can be seen quickly and plausibly without forcing the blot contours.
- Use [scoring-input/fq/none](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fnone) only when no codable form quality should be assigned.

## Cautions

- `FQ` is not the same as [scoring-input/dq](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq). `DQ` is about organization; `FQ` is about form fit.
- `FQ+` is uncommon. A response is not `+` just because it sounds rich or clever.
- The most delicate distinction outside the table is often between [scoring-input/fq/u](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fu) and [scoring-input/fq/-](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F-).
- `none` does not mean poor form. It means no form quality code should be assigned.
- A blank input is unfinished coding, not `none`; select `none` explicitly when it applies.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Form Quality] +](ref://scoring-input/fq/%2B)

- [[Coding/Form Quality] u](ref://scoring-input/fq/u)

- [[Coding/Form Quality] none](ref://scoring-input/fq/none)

# [Coding/Form Quality] +

## Aliases

- FQ+
- plus form quality
- elaborated good fit

## Definition

`FQ+` is used when the response shows good form fit and a more detailed or elaborated formal articulation than ordinary good responses.
It is both well fitted and especially well specified.

## Conditions

- The response already shows good baseline form fit.
- The subject articulates form features in a richer or more precise way than ordinary good responses.
- The elaboration improves the response without losing formal fit.
- `FQ+` remains less common than [scoring-input/fq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fo).

## Cautions

- A response is not `FQ+` just because it sounds complex or imaginative. The improvement must be formal.
- If the response is good but not clearly more elaborated than ordinary good fit, use [scoring-input/fq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fo).
- `FQ+` is not the same as [scoring-input/dq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2F%2B). One concerns form fit, the other organizational synthesis.

# [Coding/Form Quality] -

## Aliases

- FQ-
- minus
- poor form fit

## Definition

`FQ-` is assigned when the described object does not adequately fit the blot area and the response forces contours or creates features that are not really there.
It is the poor or distorted form-fit category.

## Conditions

- The object is not seen quickly or easily.
- The response depends on arbitrary contours or substantial distortion.
- Table guidance or extrapolation does not support acceptable fit.
- In doubtful off-table cases, the manual prefers `-` over overvaluing the fit.

## Cautions

- `FQ-` should not be assigned for mere unusualness. The core issue is poor fit.
- If the response is unusual but still plausible and reasonably easy to see, use [scoring-input/fq/u](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fu).
- One or two isolated `-` responses do not settle interpretation by themselves; pattern and frequency still matter.

## Cross References

- [[Coding/Form Quality] u](ref://scoring-input/fq/u)

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Form Quality] none

## Aliases

- FQnone
- no form quality code
- no FQ

## Definition

`none` is used when the response does not receive a form quality code.
This means form is not available as a codable basis for judging form fit.
A blank field is unfinished coding, not `FQnone`; select `none` explicitly when it applies.

## Conditions

- The response does not provide usable form basis for assigning `+`, `o`, `u`, or `-`.
- The code is used to separate these responses from those that do receive a specific FQ.
- Apply it cautiously and only when form quality truly should not be coded.

## Cautions

- `none` is not the same as [scoring-input/fq/-](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F-). `-` means poor fit; `none` means no FQ code applies.
- Do not change a poor-fit response into `none` just because it is difficult.
- Check the involved determinants before deciding that no codable FQ is present.

# [Coding/Form Quality] o

## Aliases

- FQo
- ordinary form quality
- good ordinary fit

## Definition

`FQo` is used when the response shows acceptable and ordinary good fit to the blot.
It is the standard good-fit category and the most common positive FQ code.

## Conditions

- The object can be seen with reasonable speed and plausibility.
- The fit is acceptable without major distortion or forcing.
- The response does not show the extra elaboration needed for `FQ+`.
- The response is more clearly fitting than `FQu`.

## Cautions

- If the response is especially well articulated beyond ordinary good fit, use [scoring-input/fq/+](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F%2B).
- If the response is unusual but still plausible, consider [scoring-input/fq/u](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fu).
- `FQo` is not the same as [scoring-input/dq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq%2Fo). One is form fit, the other is developmental quality.

# [Coding/Form Quality] u

## Aliases

- FQu
- unusual form quality
- unusual but plausible fit

## Definition

`FQu` is used when the response is uncommon or unusual, but still plausible and supportable by the blot area.
It is unusual fit, not distorted fit.

## Conditions

- The response is less common than ordinary good-fit responses.
- The object can still be seen as plausible without major forcing.
- The fit remains supportable even if it is not the most immediate reading.
- The response does not cross into clear distortion.

## Cautions

- `FQu` should not be used just because a response is creative. The fit must still be supportable.
- If the response is ordinary and clearly fitting, use [scoring-input/fq/o](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2Fo).
- If the response depends on forced contours or clear distortion, use [scoring-input/fq/-](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq%2F-).

en.title: [Coding/GHR-PHR] GHR/PHR
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/GHR-PHR] GHR/PHR

## Aliases

- GHR/PHR
- human representation
- good human representation
- poor human representation

## Definition

`GHR` and `PHR` are special codes used to qualify the quality of a human representational response.  
They are not assigned from general clinical impression, but through a decision sequence built from other codes already assigned.

## Conditions

- First confirm that the response falls in the human representational domain.
- That can happen through human content, determinant `M`, or an `FM` response carrying [scoring-input/special-score/COP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCOP) or [scoring-input/special-score/AG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAG).
- Then follow the decision sequence to determine whether the response ends in [scoring-input/gphr/GHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FGHR) or [scoring-input/gphr/PHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FPHR).
- The final decision depends on form quality, cognitive special scores, `AG`, `MOR`, `An`, `Hd`, popularity, and other signals that were already coded.

## Cautions

- `GHR` and `PHR` are not assigned together; the response ends in one or the other.
- Human content alone is not enough to settle the code.
- `GHR` does not mean "good person" and `PHR` does not mean "bad person"; they are system-level classifications of human representation.
- These decisions later feed variables such as [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/HumanCont](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FHumanCont), [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/PureH](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FPureH), and [result-interpretation/lower-section/selfPerception/H_ratio](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2FselfPerception%2FH_ratio).

en.title: [Coding/GHR-PHR] GHR
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/GHR-PHR] GHR

## Aliases

- GHR
- good human representation
- good human representational response

## Definition

`GHR` marks a human representational response that is relatively more integrated or adaptive within the system's decision sequence.  
It is not a free clinical judgment, but the result of moving through the sequence without being captured by the criteria that push toward `PHR`.

## Conditions

- First confirm that the response belongs to the human representational domain.
- A strong `GHR` case is a pure `H` response with `FQ+`, `FQo`, or `FQu`, without major cognitive special scores and without [scoring-input/special-score/AG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAG) or [scoring-input/special-score/MOR](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FMOR).
- A response with [scoring-input/special-score/COP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCOP) may also end in `GHR` as long as it does not carry `AG`.
- Popular responses on Cards III, IV, VII, and IX can also push toward `GHR` if no earlier `PHR` criterion has already captured the response.
- If no `PHR` criterion captures it first, the remaining human representational response ends in `GHR`.

## Cautions

- `GHR` is not assigned just because the response feels socially pleasant.
- `H` by itself does not guarantee `GHR`; form quality and special scores still matter.
- If aggression, morbid content, poor form, or strong cognitive special scores appear, review [scoring-input/gphr/PHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FPHR) first.
- The decision is always made inside the sequence, not from one loose rule.

en.title: [Coding/GHR-PHR] PHR
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/GHR-PHR] PHR

## Aliases

- PHR
- poor human representation
- poor human representational response

## Definition

`PHR` marks a human representational response that is relatively poorer, more distorted, or more fragile within the system's decision sequence.  
Like `GHR`, it is not chosen from free impression, but by moving through successive criteria.

## Conditions

- The response first has to qualify as a human representational response.
- `PHR` is assigned early if there is `FQ-`, `FQ none`, `ALOG`, `CONTAM`, or any level-2 cognitive special score.
- Codes such as `FABCOM`, [scoring-input/special-score/MOR](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FMOR), content [scoring-input/contents/An](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAn), [scoring-input/special-score/AG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAG), `INCOM`, `DR`, or content [scoring-input/contents/Hd](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHd) can also push toward `PHR` at the relevant point in the sequence.
- If a `PHR` criterion appears before a `GHR` criterion, the decision closes at `PHR`.

## Cautions

- `PHR` does not simply mean "negative content"; it is a classification of human representational quality.
- Not every response with `Hd` is automatically decided at once; the full sequence still matters, even though `Hd` is an important signal.
- `PHR` and `GHR` are not doubled; the response ends in one or the other.
- Later interpretation should rely on the whole protocol, not on `PHR` in isolation.

## Cross References

en.title: [Coding/Location] Location
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Location] Location

## Aliases

- Location
- location coding
- `W`, `WS`, `D`, `DS`, `Dd`, `DdS`, `S`

## Definition

Location codes which part of the blot the person uses to build the response.
The main question is whether the person uses the whole blot, a common detail, an uncommon detail, and whether white space is integrated.

## Conditions

- Fix the location precisely on the location sheet or in inquiry.
- If the whole blot is used, code [scoring-input/location/W](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FW).
- If a commonly used detail is used, code [scoring-input/location/D](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FD).
- If an infrequently used detail is used, code [scoring-input/location/Dd](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FDd).
- If white space is integrated, add `S` to the basic code: [scoring-input/location/WS](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FWS), [scoring-input/location/DS](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FDS), [scoring-input/location/DdS](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FDdS).
- `S` does not stand alone as a basic location code; it modifies another location decision.

## Cautions

- Location does not describe organization or form fit. Those are coded separately in [scoring-input/dq](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq) and [scoring-input/fq](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq).
- `D` and `Dd` are not separated by size alone; the distinction is based on common versus uncommon use of the area.
- White space should not be assumed. It must play a real role in the response.
- In interpretation, frequencies of `W`, `D`, `Dd`, and `S` reappear in the upper section of the Structural Summary.

# [Coding/Location] D

## Aliases

- D
- common detail
- usual detail location

## Definition

`D` is used when the response is based on a commonly used blot detail.
The code is about frequency of area use, not simply about the physical size of the area.

## Conditions

- The response is based on a blot area commonly used by respondents.
- The area is confirmed on the location sheet or in inquiry.
- The response does not require whole-blot use or uncommon-detail coding.

## Cautions

- `D` and `Dd` are separated by common versus uncommon use, not by “big” versus “small.”
- If white space is meaningfully integrated with the common detail, use [scoring-input/location/DS](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation%2FDS).
- `D` does not imply simplicity or normality by itself.

# [Coding/Location] S

## Aliases

- S
- white space use
- space integration

## Definition

`S` indicates meaningful use of white space in the response.
It is not a stand-alone basic location code; it modifies another location decision.

## Conditions

- White space is actively used as part of the percept.
- The role of white space is confirmed in inquiry.
- Attach `S` to the relevant basic location code: `WS`, `DS`, or `DdS`.

## Cautions

- Mentioning background alone is not enough. White space has to function as part of the percept.
- `S` should not be coded by itself as if it were a complete location decision.
- In the Structural Summary, `S` is the code that tallies white-space use; each individual response is recorded as `WS`, `DS`, or `DdS`.
- Interpretation of `S` belongs to the Structural Summary pattern, not to location coding alone.

# [Coding/Pair] Pair

## Aliases

- Pair
- (2)
- pair response
- symmetry pair

## Definition

`(2)` is used when the person perceives two identical objects from the symmetry of the card.
The key is not just that there are two things, but that they are treated as an equivalent pair derived from symmetrical organization.

## Conditions

- The response describes two identical or essentially equivalent objects.
- The perception of the pair depends on card symmetry.
- Add the code when the idea of a pair is a real part of what the person saw.
- Base the decision on the response and inquiry, not on examiner inference alone.

## Cautions

- `Pair` is not assigned simply because two different objects appear in the response.
- If the response depends on reflection, first distinguish it from [scoring-input/determinants/Fr](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFr) or [scoring-input/determinants/rF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FrF).
- `(2)` is a coding decision; its interpretive meaning is reviewed later in the Egocentricity Index.
- Not every bilateral or doubled response deserves `(2)`; the two percepts must be equivalent.

## Cross References

# [Coding/Popular] Popular

## Aliases

- Popular
- P
- popular response
- conventional response

## Definition

`Popular` identifies responses that occur with high frequency in the system’s reference population.
In coding, `P` is assigned when the response matches a defined popular by criterion, location, and content.

## Conditions

- The response must match a recognized popular response in the system.
- It is not enough for the response to resemble a popular; it must actually fit the criterion and required location.
- `P` is marked separately alongside the main response coding.
- The decision should be made from the system’s popular list, not from clinical intuition alone.

## Cautions

- A quasi-popular should not receive `P` if content or location changes in a meaningful way.
- Card orientation can matter because some populars require the top or head area to remain in the expected position.
- Frequency or absence of `P` is interpreted later; in coding, the only question is whether the response meets the criterion.
- Cultural context may affect interpretation, but the coding decision must follow the applicable Comprehensive System criterion.

## Cross References

- [[Coding] score](ref://scoring-input/score)

- [[Coding/GHR-PHR] GHR](ref://scoring-input/gphr/GHR)

en.title: [Coding] score
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding] score

## Aliases

- score
- coding
- response scoring
- code a response

## Definition

`score` does not mean assigning an immediate numeric point value.
In the Comprehensive System, it means converting each Rorschach response into a precise combination of codes.

## Conditions

- Code each response in the order it appears in the protocol.
- Coding should fix location, developmental quality, determinants, form quality, contents, and additional codes when needed.
- Inquiry should clarify the response enough so that coding represents what the person actually saw.
- Structural Summary accuracy depends on consistent response coding.

## Cautions

- `score` is not a separate numeric scale outside the protocol; it is the full response-coding process.
- Do not guess a code just because it seems likely. If inquiry does not support it, do not assign it.
- Coding and interpretation are separate stages. First code the response; then interpret the protocol results.
- Coding components are decided through different routes, such as [scoring-input/location](ref://scoring-input%2Flocation), [scoring-input/dq](ref://scoring-input%2Fdq), [scoring-input/determinants](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants), [scoring-input/fq](ref://scoring-input%2Ffq), and [scoring-input/contents](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents).

en.title: [Coding/Special Scores] Special Scores
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Special Scores] Special Scores

## Aliases

- Special Scores
- special scores
- special coding
- special score codes

## Definition

`Special Scores` are supplementary codes that capture qualities of a response that are not described fully by location, DQ, determinant, FQ, or content alone.

## Conditions

- Special Scores are added on top of the main coding; they do not replace location, determinants, or content.
- Assign them only when the special quality is clearly present in the response.
- For `DV1/DV2`, `DR1/DR2`, `INCOM1/INCOM2`, and `FABCOM1/FABCOM2`, record only one level from each pair within a response. If the level is uncertain, use Level 1 conservatively.
- Different critical Special Scores may be recorded together only when each rests on discrete wording. If the same wording or the same instance of cognitive confusion meets overlapping criteria, record only the score with the higher `WSum6` weight.
- Review the code-specific criteria for [scoring-input/special-score/COP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCOP), [scoring-input/special-score/AG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAG), [scoring-input/special-score/MOR](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FMOR), [scoring-input/special-score/AB](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FAB), [scoring-input/special-score/PSV](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FPSV), [scoring-input/special-score/PER](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FPER), [scoring-input/special-score/CP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCP), [scoring-input/special-score/DV1](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FDV1), [scoring-input/special-score/DV2](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FDV2), [scoring-input/special-score/DR1](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FDR1), [scoring-input/special-score/DR2](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FDR2), [scoring-input/special-score/INCOM1](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FINCOM1), [scoring-input/special-score/INCOM2](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FINCOM2), [scoring-input/special-score/FABCOM1](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FFABCOM1), [scoring-input/special-score/FABCOM2](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FFABCOM2), [scoring-input/special-score/CONTAM](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCONTAM), and [scoring-input/special-score/ALOG](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FALOG).
- `COP` and `AG` depend on movement content, usually [scoring-input/determinants/M](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FM), [scoring-input/determinants/FM](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFM), or [scoring-input/determinants/m](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2Fm).
- `MOR` is added when damage, deterioration, death, or a distinctly morbid quality is attributed to the object.
- `AB` is used for abstract formulation and often needs review together with [scoring-input/contents/Hx](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHx), [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt), and [scoring-input/contents/Ay](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAy).
- `PSV` is used for perseveration and later connects with the interpretation route [result-interpretation/lower-section/processing/PSV](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fprocessing%2FPSV).
- `PER` is used for personalized justification and later connects with [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/PER](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FPER) and [result-interpretation/lower-section/mediation/Xu_percent](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fmediation%2FXu_percent).
- `CP` is used for projected chromatic color in an achromatic area and should be reviewed alongside [scoring-input/determinants/FC](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFC), [scoring-input/determinants/FY](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFY), [scoring-input/determinants/YF](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FYF), [scoring-input/determinants/Y](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FY), and the later interpretation route [result-interpretation/lower-section/affect/CP](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Faffect%2FCP).
- `DV1` and `DV2` are used for deviant verbalization and later connect with [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/Sum6](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FSum6), [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/Lv2](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FLv2), and [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/WSum6](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FWSum6).
- `DR1` and `DR2` are used for deviant response organization and should be separated from `DV1 / DV2`, which focus more on verbal formulation itself.
- `INCOM1` and `INCOM2` are used for incongruous combinations and should be separated from both `FABCOM` and `CONTAM`.
- `FABCOM1` and `FABCOM2` are used for fabulized relations among response elements and should be separated from `INCOM` and `CONTAM`.
- `CONTAM` is used for contaminated fusion of incompatible percepts within one response.
- `ALOG` is used for inappropriate or insufficient logic used to justify a response.
- These codes later connect to interpretation routes such as [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/COP](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FCOP), [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/AG](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FAG), [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/MOR](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FMOR), [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/_2AB_Art_Ay](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2F_2AB_Art_Ay), [result-interpretation/lower-section/interpersonal/PER](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Finterpersonal%2FPER), [result-interpretation/lower-section/affect/CP](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Faffect%2FCP), [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/Sum6](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FSum6), [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/Lv2](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FLv2), and [result-interpretation/lower-section/ideation/WSum6](ref://result-interpretation%2Flower-section%2Fideation%2FWSum6).

## Cautions

- A Special Score should not be used as a vague overall impression; it requires an observable feature in the response.
- `COP` and `AG` are not assigned just because two figures are present; there must be clearly cooperative or aggressive action.
- `MOR` does not mean any sad or unpleasant content; it requires death, damage, deterioration, ruin, or another directly morbid quality.
- `AB` should not become a catch-all for any unusual or symbolic answer.
- `PSV` does not mean simple consistency or thematic preference; it requires perseverative repetition.
- `PER` is not assigned just because the subject says "I" or makes a loose autobiographical comment.
- `CP` should not be mixed with normal chromatic determinants when color has been projected onto an achromatic area.
- `DV1` and `DV2` differ by severity of verbal deviation and should not automatically be confused with `DR1` or `DR2`.
- `DR1` and `DR2` are not assigned just because a response is long; they require a deviation in the organization of the full response.
- `INCOM1` and `INCOM2` are not synonyms for fantasy or creativity; they require a genuinely incongruous combination.
- `FABCOM1` and `FABCOM2` are not catch-all labels for imagination; they require an implausible relation among elements.
- `CONTAM` requires real perceptual contamination, not just a striking metaphor.
- `ALOG` requires faulty inference, not merely unusual wording.
- Human content may later connect with [scoring-input/gphr/GHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FGHR) or [scoring-input/gphr/PHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FPHR), but Special Scores do not decide those codes by themselves.

# [Coding/Special Scores] AB

## Aliases

- AB
- abstractions
- abstract response

## Definition

`AB` is coded when the response moves away from a concrete object and shifts into an abstract, generalized, or loosely conceptual formulation.  
The key point is that the subject names an abstraction or broad quality rather than a clearly bounded object.

## Conditions

- Consider `AB` when the response names something like an emotion, an idea, a force, a sensation, or another abstract formulation.
- It may appear near [scoring-input/contents/Hx](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FHx) when the response points to generalized human experience rather than a specific person.
- It may also coexist with [scoring-input/contents/Art](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FArt) or [scoring-input/contents/Ay](ref://scoring-input%2Fcontents%2FAy) when the subject turns the content into a highly abstract category.
- This is added as a Special Score and does not replace the main content code.

## Cautions

- Not every symbolic or artistic response receives `AB`.
- `Hx` by itself does not require `AB`; the wording has to be genuinely abstract.
- A response that is unusual but still concrete should not receive `AB` just because it sounds sophisticated.

## Cross References

en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Special Scores] AG

## Aliases

- AG
- aggressive movement
- aggressive action

## Definition

`AG` is coded when a movement response shows clearly aggressive action.  
What matters is aggression as an ongoing act, not just a vague hostile quality of the object.

## Conditions

- The response must include movement, usually [scoring-input/determinants/M](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FM), [scoring-input/determinants/FM](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2FFM), or [scoring-input/determinants/m](ref://scoring-input%2Fdeterminants%2Fm).
- The action has to be observably aggressive: striking, attacking, tearing, violently pushing, biting, or injuring.
- The code is used for aggression as movement, not merely for damage that has already happened.
- If the aggressive action is carried out jointly by more than one figure, `AG` may coexist with [scoring-input/special-score/COP](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FCOP).

## Cautions

- A hostile adjective without clear action does not justify `AG`.
- If the main focus is that the object is already broken, dead, or deteriorated, first reconsider [scoring-input/special-score/MOR](ref://scoring-input%2Fspecial-score%2FMOR).
- `AG` does not automatically decide [scoring-input/gphr/PHR](ref://scoring-input%2Fgphr%2FPHR); that decision requires an additional coding step.

en.title: [Coding/Special Scores] ALOG
en.bodyMarkdown:
# [Coding/Special Scores] ALOG

## Aliases

- ALOG
- inappropriate logic
- faulty logic

## Definition

`ALOG` is coded when the person supports the response with logic that is improper or clearly insufficient.  
The focus is on an unjustified inference, not on a strange word or a perceptual mixture.

## Conditions

- Use `ALOG` when the explanation or justification of the response shows an inappropriate logical leap.
- The conclusion being offered should sound poorly supported even within the subject's own framework.
- The problem lies in the logic used to support the idea, not only in verbal form.
- `ALOG` contributes to `Sum6` and may later influence `WSum6`.

## Cautions

- Do not assign `ALOG` just for unusual style, dramatized tone, or a response that is hard to follow.
- If the main oddity lies in a deviant word or phrase, compare it with `DV1` first.
- If the deviation affects the global organization of the response, also compare it with `DR1`.
- Responses induced by follow-up questioning should not automatically be turned into `ALOG`.
